t: Substrings of Size Three with Distinct Characters — Fixed-Size Window Checks
o:
**Understanding the problem**

A substring is good when all of its characters are distinct, and we must count the good substrings of length exactly 3. Repeated occurrences count separately — every starting index contributes independently.

**Walking through Example 1:** s = xyzzaz has four windows: xyz (distinct — good), yzz (repeated z), zza (repeated z), and zaz (repeated z). Exactly one good window, so the answer is 1.

**Example 2:** s = aababcabc yields seven windows aab, aba, bab, abc, bca, cab, abc; the last four are good (abc appears twice at different positions), giving 4.

**What the constraints imply:** with n <= 100 even checking every window with a fresh set is instant. More instructively, because the window length is fixed at 3, distinctness is equivalent to three pairwise comparisons s[i] != s[i+1], s[i+1] != s[i+2], s[i] != s[i+2] — no auxiliary structure needed.
k: There are n - 2 windows of length 3; slide over each starting index once.
A 3-character window is all-distinct if and only if the first two characters differ AND each adjacent pair differs — pairwise inequality among three items implies global uniqueness.
Duplicate substrings still count individually: iterate positions, not unique substrings.

a.i: For every window of size 3, insert its characters into a set and compare the set's size against 3 — a set collapses duplicates, so equality means all characters were distinct. This generalizes immediately to any window length k by asking for size k, making it the natural template to reach for before specializing to constant-time tricks.
s: For each i from 0 to len(s) - 3, build the window s[i..i+2].
Add its characters to a set; if the set contains 3 elements, increment the counter.
a.t: O(n) — n - 2 windows, each processed in O(3) time for set insertion.
a.sp: O(1) — each set holds at most 3 characters.

a.n: Approach 2: Pairwise Comparisons (Constant Work per Window)
a.i: With only three characters, uniqueness can be decided directly: the window is good exactly when no two of its positions match, which is three comparisons. This removes set construction entirely and makes the per-window cost truly constant with tiny constants — the optimal specialization for this fixed size.
s: For each i from 0 to len(s) - 3, test s[i] != s[i+1], s[i+1] != s[i+2], and s[i] != s[i+2].
Increment the counter whenever all three hold.
a.t: O(n) — one pass doing exactly three character comparisons per window.

w: Lead with Approach 1 to show the sliding-window/set pattern, then note that a fixed width of 3 collapses to three inequalities — Approach 2 is what you would actually ship. Pitfalls: off-by-one loop bounds (the last valid start is n - 3, so guard with i + 2 < n), and remembering that identical substrings at different positions each count (Example 2's double abc). Edge cases: strings shorter than 3 have zero windows and answer 0. Follow-ups: generalize to windows of length k with all-distinct characters using a frequency map and a variable-size sliding window in O(n) total, or count good substrings of ANY length.
